topic: Extensible Software in the Age of LLMs
summary: Jeremy Morrell's Aug 2026 essay argues web software is frozen at the head of the demand curve, LLMs have made 'software for one' cheap, and the remaining gap is a safe, shareable extension point on the web. The 2026 evidence (MCP at 9,264 npm-keyword packages and 11k-23k registry servers, WordPress at 69,937 plugins, agent harnesses shipping 68 internal plugins) shows extension supply is no longer the bottleneck - trust, versioning, discovery and distribution are. The practice guidance: keep a small accountable core, hand untrusted extension code a narrow capability instead of a credential, and buy a sandbox primitive with ~$0 idle cost, single-digit-ms cold start and enforceable limits.
key_takeaways: Extensibility is a product-boundary decision before it is a runtime decision: the constraint that used to kill one-user features (a week of engineering) is gone, so 'conceptual integrity' has to replace it.
Hand untrusted extension code a capability (one approved function) rather than a token plus a filtering proxy - Morrell: 'the code can only take actions via the references it has been passed'.
Extension points are the durable API surface: Pi (tools/commands/events/UI), Claude Code (skills/agents/hooks/MCP + plugin.json), opencode (JS/TS hook modules loaded from disk or npm).

A safe extension runtime has the same requirements as an agent sandbox: ~$0 idle cost, single-digit-ms cold start, hard CPU/memory/network/log limits, fault + security isolation including Spectre, and narrow action surface.

Local plugin culture (Obsidian, IDEs, game mods, CAD) proves authorship works but exposes the trust problem - Obsidian plugins can do anything; that tradeoff collapses once the data belongs to other people.
Distribution, not authoring, is the 2026 bottleneck: only 0.07% of 79,827 agent-economy listings carry a price, and versioning/sharing/source control inside the product is listed as table stakes.

key_points: Primary source (Aug 18, 2026; 177 pts / 88 comments on Hacker News). Morrell works at Cloudflare and discloses it.

Thesis: web software is static because attention is finite and every added feature taxes every other user; the top of the demand curve is well served, the long tail is not. LLMs made 'Software for One' cheap, so the gap is no longer building a personal tool - it is deploying, securing and sharing it.

Coins 'LLM-native software' with Pi as the example: a battle-tested core that is almost endlessly extensible just by asking, where users share their customizations. Extension requests are plain prose ('send every article I fave longer than 4000 words to my e-reader').
Names four frontiers: AI agents, internal corporate platforms, support platforms, observability platforms - each currently served by webhooks that force you to run a separate service.

Security argument: extensibility on the web is hard (infinite loops taking down the service, key forwarding to a third party, sensitive-data exfiltration, DoS in both directions, Spectre, free-compute crypto mining). Obsidian is cited as the model that works only because stakes are low - 'a plugin can basically do anything'.

Precedent: Salesforce has run this pattern since 2007 as a multi-tenant programmable platform (Apex, @RestResource HTTP endpoints, Schedulable cron, USER_MODE, tenant isolation, no webserver to deploy) - 'a precursor to modern serverless'. AWS S3/EC2 shipped in 2006, for reference.

Requirement list for 'a new primitive': cheap (~$0 when idle, tiny fractions of a cent per execution), fast cold starts (single-digit ms), control over limits (CPU, memory, network request count/size, response size, log volume), a solid fault + security isolation boundary, and a safe way to take actions.

Rejects ambient I/O and the token-broker proxy as the default: filtering logic for one operation on one endpoint is already large, and 'starting with a lot of power and then trying to restrict it precisely is a hard problem'. Wants capabilities: 'If we remove ambient I/O, the code can only take actions via the references it has been passed.' IFTTT analogy - you get twitter.post_new_tweet(), not a Twitter API key.
Notes capabilities are also better for LLMs: generating logic from a TypeScript definition of capabilities is easier and more token-efficient than handing the model a pile of OpenAPI JSON.

Technology survey: embeddable interpreters (Lua, QuickJS, roll-your-own); V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers/workerd, celld, isolated-vm, Rivet secure-exec); microVMs (Firecracker, libkrun, AWS Lambda MicroVMs, @deno/sandbox, smolvm, Tensorlake, Daytona) for POSIX + full binaries at ~1s start; WASM + WASI because it starts from a blank slate and the host defines passed capabilities; and Cap'n Web as an object-capability RPC protocol on top of any of them.

Recommends Cloudflare Dynamic Workers as the closest production-ready fit in 2026 while noting it is 'an ad for sandboxes + the idea of OCaps' (author's own HN reply), and lists what you still build yourself: observability (OpenTelemetry in the runtime), per-user SQLite/Durable Object facets or R2 buckets, durable execution (Dynamic Workflows), source control built into the product, hosted LLMs with token budgets, and in-runtime JS transpilation (sucrase) so extension authoring needs no separate VM.

Honest limits: 'Platforms are hard: hard to design, hard to run, hard to debug' and footnote 1 concedes participation inequality - a small percentage will author most extensions no matter how easy authoring becomes.
Independent digest (Aug 20, 2026) that reframes the essay as a product-boundary rule: 'A solid core plus sandboxed extensions beats a fatter product.'
The product lesson it extracts: 'It is not let the agent rewrite the app. Keep the core boring and let the long tail live outside it.'

Connects Morrell to Simon Willison on conceptual integrity and counting lines of code: agents deleted the old veto (time), so conceptual integrity must replace it - 'if the request is a one-user bump, do not merge it into the core'.
Useful framing for a blog outline: the extension point is where you spend your design budget instead of on features.

Daily-report synthesis that positions the essay one layer above AGENTS.md: 'If AGENTS.md is the contract for coding agents, this is the same idea one layer up: software that expects to be completed by the person using it.'
Its one-line summary of the economics: 'LLMs changed the economics of the long tail: people can now ask for a one-off tool and get it.'
Useful quotable framing for an intro/conclusion; low original reporting value otherwise.
Interactive explainer of Morrell's essay (subtitle: 'a visual explainer'), produced as a one-shot demo by another model - evidence the thesis is being dogfooded as web extension content.
Its chapter structure doubles as a competitor outline: the long tail, LLM-native software, 'four frontiers', and the opencode 68-internal-plugins proof point.

Quotes the opencode claim in full: 'nearly everything is an internal plugin - there's 68 of them that cover our built-in agents, integrations, config loading... you can disable any behavior and we also properly dogfood our plugin apis' (opencode, Aug 13, 2026).
Frames the catch as tooling the product must own: built-in source control/versioning for extensions, hosted LLMs with token budgets and rate limits, and self-hosted JS tooling.
SelfEvolve (arXiv 2604.16314, Feb 2026): an agentic pipeline for runtime self-extension - adding new capabilities during execution with no restart and no developer intervention.
Measured result: average Pass@1 92.7% (51/55) across 11 self-extension tasks, 61.8% better than the best baseline (AutoGen) with statistical significance; MetaGPT and AgentCoder also beaten.

Mechanism worth citing: generated function is verified in a sandbox, then promoted into the running system (importlib.reload()) and added to a knowledge base for reuse - i.e. generated extensions become durable artifacts.

States the open risks plainly: a newly integrated function does not guarantee the rest of the system stays correct; the paper mitigates with novel-code evaluation and points to model diversity as future work.
OpenHands Software Agent SDK (arXiv 2511.03690): a composable, extensible foundation for production agents, and a documented rewrite story about what extensibility costs when it is bolted on.

The V0 failure mode is the cautionary data point: ad hoc extensions produced 'severe sprawl - 140+ fields, 15 classes, and 2.8K lines of configuration code - a brittle system where small changes often cascaded into unrelated failures'.

V1 design rules map almost one-to-one onto app extensibility: stateless by default with one source of truth for state; strict separation of concerns so the core evolves independently; a typed component model where developers extend or reconfigure declaratively without touching the core.
Compatibility claim worth repeating: external MCP tools behave identically to native tools, and sandboxing is opt-in rather than universal.
Vendor-side treatment of the plugin-as-extension-point pattern (Semantic Kernel): the kernel discovers, invokes and manages capabilities that are wrapped as standardized plugins.

Benefits it claims are the same ones an app-level extension system wants: modular integration, declarative invocation via descriptions the model can select on, a unified interface, centralized monitoring (token usage, execution flow) and simplified result aggregation.

Concrete mechanism for a 'how does this actually work' section: plugin descriptions via decorators are what let the orchestrator pick the right capability, plus per-plugin token accounting across invoked plugins.

stats.fact: The source essay hit the Hacker News front page at 177 points and 88 comments on 2026-08-19 (posted 2026-08-18) - and the author (masterj) and Kenton Varda both replied in the thread, which is where the sandbox/OCap details and the 'it reads like an ad for Cloudflare' critique live.

opencode refactored so that nearly everything is an internal plugin: 68 of them covering built-in agents, integrations and config loading, all individually disableable - 'we also properly dogfood our plugin apis'.
stats.source: opencode (@thdxr / dax), Aug 13, 2026, quoted in the Morrell essay and in the Sulat explainer

stats.fact: opencode (anomalyco/opencode) sits at 211,057 GitHub stars and 27,956 forks, MIT licensed, TypeScript - the largest single artifact in this story.
The official MCP reference server repo (modelcontextprotocol/servers) is at 90,712 stars and 11,717 forks.

MCP SDK download growth: the npm TypeScript SDK went from ~38.5M monthly downloads in Dec 2025 to ~204M by Sep 1 2026, and the PyPI mcp package adds ~319M/month - roughly 5x in nine months, against the ~97M/month combined figure cited at the Linux Foundation donation (Dec 9, 2025). The project now cites 'close to half a billion downloads a month' across Tier 1 SDKs.
stats.source: agentscamp.com MCP ecosystem statistics, aggregating npm registry API and pypistats, snapshot Sep 1, 2026

stats.fact: MCP server counts depend entirely on the registry you cite, which is why a bare number is misleading: Smithery 11,245 (up from 6,652 in July 2026), PulseMCP 21,982, mcp.so ~23,000 (self-reported, Jul 1 2026).
stats.source: agentscamp.com compilation of registry APIs, Sep 1, 2026; corroborated by a16y.ai (PulseMCP 12,900+ earlier in 2026)

stats.fact: npm carries 9,264 packages keyworded 'mcp-server' as of 2026-09-30, versus 556 for 'claude-code-plugin' and 2,186 for 'opencode-plugin' - the agent-extension package economy today is mostly MCP-shaped.

Classic web extension ecosystems for scale comparison, all read directly on 2026-09-30: WordPress.org directory 69,937 plugins; Obsidian community plugins 8,241 (obsidian-releases community-plugins.json); Firefox add-ons (AMO) 621,529 total; Shopify App Store advertises '16,000 apps' on its own homepage.

stats.fact: Cloudflare's Code Mode pitch - convert MCP tools into a TypeScript API and let the LLM write code that calls it, instead of exposing tools directly - is claimed to let agents handle many more tools and to save 'up to 80% in inference tokens and cost' by processing data programmatically instead of round-tripping it through the model.
stats.source: Cloudflare blog 'Code Mode: the better way to use MCP' (Kenton Varda and Sunil Pai, Sep 26, 2025); restated in the Dynamic Workers docs (updated Apr 21, 2026)

stats.fact: Cloudflare Dynamic Workers is positioned explicitly as the extension-platform primitive: spin up an unlimited number of Workers at runtime to execute arbitrary code with a caller-defined composition, bindings, network access and observability, described as 'a lightweight alternative to containers for securely sandboxing code you don't trust'. The underlying runtime (cloudflare/workerd) is 8,791 stars, Apache-2.0, C++.

The MCP spec itself was donated to the Linux Foundation on Dec 9, 2025; the Agentic AI Foundation went from 49 founding members to 247 by Aug 13, 2026, with Platinum capped at eight (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, AWS, Block and others).
stats.source: agentscamp.com citing Linux Foundation announcements, Aug 13, 2026

stats.fact: Agent-extension economy census (2026-08-12): 79,848 listings - 58,766 agent skills, 8,433 MCP servers, 10,264 marketplaces, 2,385 plugins - with 164,841,042 cumulative installs, ~35,931 installs/day, and only 55 of 79,827 listings (0.07%) carrying a price; 1,404 listings ask users to bring their own API key.
stats.source: skillselion.com AI Agent Statistics, aggregating the Agent Skill Security / Agent Economy censuses of Aug 9-12, 2026

stats.fact: Directory-layer counts from an independent market view (May 2026): claudemarketplaces.com listed 4,200+ skills, 2,500+ marketplaces and 770+ MCP servers, framed as 'GitHub repositories that collect and distribute plugins... acts as a registry you can subscribe to for skills, MCP servers, commands, hooks, and agents'.

Obsidian's extension model works only because the stakes are low: plugins are effectively unrestricted ('a plugin can basically do anything'), and the project defends itself with automated and manual review plus verified authors - a tradeoff Morrell says collapses once the software holds customer records, financial transactions or private messages.
stats.source: Morrell essay, 'Extensible software on the web is... harder'

stats.fact: The capability model in production: Kenton Varda described Cloudflare OS running an app's client-side code in a null-origin iframe sandbox denied everything deniable, communicating only through a Cap'n Web RPC session over postMessage to the parent frame, with the app's own server running in a Dynamic Worker sandbox - so the client can only talk to its own server, nothing else.

Cloudflare's own framing of bindings is object-capability RPC: the essay's footnote 4 notes 'Bindings and Service Workers work on an Object Capability RPC system. You can think of exposing capabilities to users as generating bindings for your particular service.'

SelfEvolve's runtime self-extension result: 92.7% average Pass@1 (51/55) across 11 tasks, 61.8% over the best baseline (AutoGen), with generated functions promoted from a sandbox into the live system via importlib.reload() and no restart.

The cost of retrofitting extensibility after the fact, from a team that did the rewrite: OpenHands V0 ended at 140+ fields, 15 classes and 2.8K lines of configuration code, described as 'a brittle system where small changes often cascaded into unrelated failures'.

The counter-argument on the record: a top-level HN commenter argues extension-by-accumulation reproduces the complexity problem inside the host app and that the proven alternative is composing separate small programs - 'you don't add a file search extension to your application; you make one completely separate app, called grep, and call it from any application.'

angles: Frame the whole guide around a product decision, not a runtime one: the old veto on one-user features (a week of engineering) is gone, so the substitute is a named boundary - 'keep the core boring and let the long tail live outside it' (Dustcrawl/Willison). This is the differentiator most competitors skip; they jump straight to sandboxes.

Make the capability model the technical spine: contrast the token-plus-filtering-proxy pattern (which grows into per-endpoint filtering logic you can't keep bulletproof) with handing untrusted code one approved function - 'the code can only take actions via the references it has been passed' - and note the bonus that TypeScript capability definitions are more token-efficient for the model than OpenAPI JSON.

Treat extension points as the API you will maintain for years, with 2026's concrete shapes: Pi (stable hooks for tools, commands, events, UI, reloaded in place, bundled into shareable packages), Claude Code (a plugin directory of skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers declared by .claude-plugin/plugin.json, distributed through marketplaces), opencode (JS/TS modules exporting hook objects such as tool.execute.before, loaded from .opencode/plugins/ or npm and installed with bun at startup).

Ground the sandbox shopping list in the same requirements as agent execution, which the essay calls out explicitly, then walk the four primitive families with the real tradeoff each carries: interpreter (Lua/QuickJS), V8 isolates (workerd, celld, isolated-vm, Rivet secure-exec), microVMs (Firecracker, libkrun, AWS Lambda MicroVMs, @deno/sandbox, smolvm, Tensorlake, Daytona - POSIX and full binaries, but ~1s start), and WASM+WASI (blank slate, host-defined capabilities, higher toolchain complexity); Cap'n Web overlays object capabilities on any of them.

Show that the 2026 numbers move the bottleneck: extension supply is no longer the problem (9,264 npm mcp-server packages, 11k-23k registry servers depending on the bar, WordPress at 69,937 plugins, Obsidian at 8,241), so the differentiators are trust, versioning, discovery and shareability - the 0.07% priced figure is the tell that the economy is supply-rich and monetization-poor.

Use the cautionary cases as the article's credibility: Obsidian's trust-every-plugin model is fine for notes and fails for customer records; OpenHands' V0 shows the 140-field/2.8K-line config sprawl that ad hoc extension produces; SelfEvolve shows generated extensions integrating at runtime without a restart and admits the correctness risk of doing so.

Include the dissent, don't paper over it: the strongest HN objection is that extension surfaces reproduce complexity inside the host and that composing separate small programs (the grep model) is the proven alternative - a guide that names when NOT to build an extension point will outrank one that only sells the pattern.

Anchor the closing section in platform reality: Morrell has run platforms for a decade and still warns 'platforms are hard: hard to design, hard to run, hard to debug', and concedes participation inequality (a small share of users author most extensions) - so set reader expectations with a staged adoption path (versioning and source control first, then capabilities, then a sandbox primitive) rather than a big-bang platform launch.

outline: H2: Why web software stopped at the head of the demand curve (the long tail, and why every added feature taxes every other user)
H2: What changed: LLMs made software-for-one cheap, so the gap moved to deploy, secure and share
H2: LLM-native software: the Pi pattern of a battle-tested core that is extensible just by asking (and its limits outside the terminal)
H2: The boundary decision - keep the core accountable and put the long tail on an extension point ('conceptual integrity' as the replacement for the lost time veto)
H2: What a good extension point looks like in 2026 (Pi hooks, Claude Code plugin components, opencode JS hook modules, MCP tools as the distribution layer)
H2: Four places this pays off first: agents, internal corporate platforms, support platforms, observability platforms (and why webhooks are not enough)
H2: The security reality: why Obsidian's trust-every-plugin model falls apart once the data belongs to someone else
H2: Capabilities, not API keys - hand untrusted code one approved function, not a token and a filtering proxy
H2: Choosing an isolation primitive: interpreters, V8 isolates, microVMs, WASM/WASI (and the five requirements they must satisfy)
H2: What you still have to build yourself: observability, per-tenant storage, durable execution, version control, hosted LLM budgets, in-runtime transpilation
H2: The counter-argument: when a separate small app beats an in-app extension point
H2: A staged adoption path: versioning first, capabilities second, sandbox primitive third
H2: FAQ: is an extension point the same as a plugin API, do I need a microVM, how do I stop a bad extension from taking my service down, how do I let an LLM write extensions safely
H2: Sources and further reading (Morrell essay, HN thread, SelfEvolve, OpenHands SDK, Cloudflare Dynamic Workers and Code Mode)

faq.q: Is an 'extension point' just an old plugin API with a new name?
faq.a: The mechanism is familiar, the economics are not. Morrell's argument is that the authoring cost collapsed (users can now speak code into existence), so the design constraint moved from 'how do I stop feature requests' to 'where do I allow code to run and what can it touch'. A 2026 extension point is a plugin API plus a sandbox boundary plus a capability list plus in-product version control.

faq.q: Why not just give extensions a scoped API key?
faq.a: Because restricting a powerful credential precisely is the hard problem: you end up writing per-endpoint filter logic that must track every change in the backing API, and even fine-grained scopes rarely express 'only this one email'. Capabilities invert it - the code receives references it can call, holds no credential, and cannot leak or reach anything it was not handed.

faq.q: Do I need a microVM to run user extensions?
faq.a: Usually not. MicroVMs buy POSIX and full binaries at roughly a second of startup; if your extensions are logic, API calls and small workflows, a V8 isolate, an embeddable interpreter, or WASM+WASI is a better cost/latency fit. MicroVMs are still useful for authoring, bundling and testing extensions, and none of the options are mutually exclusive.

faq.q: How do I keep one bad extension from taking the service down?
faq.a: The essay lists the requirements explicitly: enforce limits on CPU, memory, network requests, response size and log volume/rate; isolate faults as well as security (infinite loops, memory bombs); and remember the Heroku lesson where a popular getting-started guide shipped while True: print('hello world!'). Limits plus a real isolation boundary are the minimum, not either one alone.

faq.q: Can I let an LLM write extensions safely?
faq.a: That is the whole point of the capability model - a narrow capability list is both a safe boundary and a better prompt surface (TypeScript capability definitions beat a pile of OpenAPI JSON for token efficiency). SelfEvolve shows runtime-generated functions can be verified in a sandbox and promoted into a running system without a restart at 92.7% Pass@1 on 11 tasks, and openly flags the correctness risk to the rest of the system.

writer_notes: Type is 'guide': prioritize decision structure (when to extend, what to expose, which primitive) over news framing. The event anchor is the Aug 18-19 2026 essay plus its HN thread; the evergreen value is the boundary/capability/sandbox checklist.

Attribute the Cloudflare material as disclosure - Morrell states he works at Cloudflare and Dynamic Workers is his recommendation; the HN thread's 'reads like an ad' critique is part of the story, not something to hide.
Always name the registry when citing MCP server counts (Smithery 11,245 / PulseMCP 21,982 / mcp.so ~23,000) - the spread is 2x and a bare number is indefensible.

Prefer the capability and boundary sections as the differentiator: competitor coverage (Dustcrawl, windflash, the Sulat explainer) stops at the product lesson and rarely goes deeper than naming Dynamic Workers.

Include at least one code-shaped illustration from the primary source: the proxy-filtering version versus the capability version, and the Salesforce Apex/Scheduled example for the 'this has worked at scale since 2007' point.
Do not present SelfEvolve or Cloudflare Code Mode numbers as vendor-neutral benchmarks without their source context (arXiv preprint; Cloudflare's own claim of up to 80% token savings).
